newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin hopeful of clearing way to Belarus union.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin hopeful of clearing way to Belarus union.

text.p: "Two or three" obstacles are still blocking a charter on union between Russia and Belarus but President Boris Yeltsin expects to overcome them in time to sign the document this week, the Kremlin said on Tuesday.

Yeltsin is due to meet Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko in Moscow on Thursday and they plan to sign the charter, deepening integration between their two former Soviet republics, the following day.
"They will make a final attack, as it were, on the document which has, in the main, been hammered out," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

"Two or three issues remain to be settled. The president has said he hopes to resolve them fairly quickly with Alexander Grigoryevich (Lukashenko) to be able to sign the Russia-Belarus union charter at 2 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Friday."
Yastrzhembsky gave no details. Lukashenko said on Monday three issues had to be resolved -- the authority of the union's governing organ, the powers its leader will have, and its location.
The two presidents signed an outline union agreement in Moscow on April 2 but left the guts of the treaty, including the more controversial points, to be defined in the separate charter.

Many Russians and Belarussians, nostalgic for the Soviet Union which collapsed more than five years ago, support the idea of union between the Russian Federation of 150 million people and its western Slav neighbour of only 10 million.

But Kremlin liberals, wary that the authoritarian Lukashenko might gain a foothold on power in Russia and act as a brake on free-market reforms, managed to have the planned union treaty watered down on the eve of the treaty signing ceremony.
Lukashenko had wanted a supranational body set up with powers to make decisions about the union, and made clear the final draft fell short of his dream.

Yeltsin has said a complete merger of the two countries is now his ultimate goal -- an idea opposed by Lukashenko, who wants a union of two equal sovereign states and would oppose any move that might see Russia swallow up little Belarus.
Discussion of the merits of the planned union at a Moscow "round table" of experts on Tuesday at times became heated.

Vladimir Pokrovsky, a member of a joint committee overseeing union, said a poll this month showed almost four in five Russians had backed the idea of union during the period set aside for public discussion after April 2.
He said the discussion had taken up 43 hours of television time, produced more than 300 newspaper articles, and inspired 50,000 letters or telephone calls to the committee.
Critics have said public discussion was limited and that a referendum on union should have been held in both countries.
Some participants at the round table suggested Moscow would end up dominating Belarus again. Others said the charter had been watered down so much that it would have little practical effect.
Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's former security adviser and now his critic, told a news conference all discussion was absurd.
"It is not even worthwhile discussing whether or not the reunification is right or wrong because it concerns two fraternal peoples who have always lived together," he said.
